metadata.title: The immigrant paradox and math self-concept: An SES-of-origin-country hypothesis

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the Australian PISA extended datasets for 2003 and 2012, which are based on PISA’s two-stage stratified sampling of schools and students within schools. The authors report that all multilevel models were weighted using the final survey weight provided in the datasets, and they include a random intercept for school to reflect the nested sampling structure. Missing data were handled via multiple imputation (Amelia II) with School ID used as the clustering variable, and results across imputations were combined using Rubin’s rules. The manuscript does not name the exact weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT), but it explicitly states that final survey weights from the OECD PISA technical documentation were applied.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the full available Australian PISA extended datasets for the 2003 and 2012 cohorts (15-year-olds; mathematics as focal domain). For immigrant status coding, the authors restricted to students with information on both parents’ countries of origin (PISA-defined immigrant status), yielding N=12,108 (PISA 2003) and N=13,889 (PISA 2012) for the immigrant-status analyses. Multiple imputation was applied to address missing data, and math achievement was represented using five plausible values with one plausible value assigned per imputed dataset, followed by pooling via Rubin’s approach.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Survey-weighted multilevel model coefficients (β) with SE; key effects include: immigrant status main effects (e.g., 1st gen β=0.196, SE=0.030; 2nd gen β=0.137, SE=0.030 in Table 1), math achievement positive (e.g., β=0.450, SE=0.011 in Table 2 Models 7B/7C), relative SES negative (e.g., β=-0.091, SE=0.011 in Table 2 Model 7F), and school-average achievement negative (e.g., β=-0.281, SE=0.027 in Table 2 Model 7F).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2003 Australia mathematics the study leveraged immigrant status, math achievement (PVs), absolute parental education, relative SES (origin-country mean years of education), and school-average achievement to predict math self-concept, finding that both first- and second-generation immigrants had higher math self-concepts than native students even after controlling for achievement, and that adding relative SES reduced the immigrant paradox (with relative SES showing a negative association with math self-concept). This indicates that contextualizing immigrants’ socioeconomic background relative to their parents’ origin country can explain part of why immigrant students report higher math self-concepts, beyond absolute SES and achievement.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Survey-weighted multilevel model coefficients (β) with SE; key effects include: immigrant status main effects (e.g., 1st gen β=0.200, SE=0.030; 2nd gen β=0.166, SE=0.033 in Table 1), math achievement positive (e.g., β=0.354, SE=0.012 in Table 3 Model 8B), relative SES negative (e.g., β=-0.065, SE=0.012 in Table 3 Model 8D), and school-average achievement negative (e.g., β=-0.223, SE=0.022 in Table 3 Model 8E).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 Australia mathematics the study leveraged immigrant status, math achievement (PVs), absolute parental education, relative SES (origin-country mean years of education), and school-average achievement to predict math self-concept, finding that immigrant students had higher math self-concepts than native students in absolute terms and that relative SES negatively predicted math self-concept while substantially reducing the immigrant paradox. This indicates that policies and school supports that consider immigrants’ origin-context socioeconomic benchmarks may better address self-concept formation than relying only on host-country absolute SES measures.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Survey-weighted multilevel model coefficients (β) with SE; key effects include: immigrant status main effects (e.g., 1st gen β=0.271, SE=0.027; 2nd gen β=0.262, SE=0.027 in Table 4), math achievement positive (e.g., β=0.321, SE=0.010 in Table 4 Model 9B), and relative SES negative (e.g., β=-0.090, SE=0.010 in Table 4 Model 9D).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2003 Australia mathematics the study leveraged immigrant status, math achievement (PVs), absolute parental education, relative SES (origin-country mean years of education), and school-average achievement to predict educational expectations, finding that immigrants had higher educational expectations than native students and that the immigrant paradox persisted when controlling for absolute SES but reduced substantially when relative SES was included. This indicates that expectation-achievement gaps for immigrant students are partly contextual and may be mitigated by interventions that help align students’ perceived academic standing with their achievement realities while acknowledging origin-context SES.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Survey-weighted multilevel model coefficients (β) with SE; key effects include: immigrant status main effects (e.g., 1st gen β=0.177, SE=0.025; 2nd gen β=0.245, SE=0.024 in Table 5 Model 10A), math achievement positive (e.g., β=0.353, SE=0.009 in Table 5 Model 10B), and relative SES negative (e.g., β=-0.043, SE=0.009 in Table 5 Model 10E).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 Australia mathematics the study leveraged immigrant status, math achievement (PVs), absolute parental education, relative SES (origin-country mean years of education), and school-average achievement to predict educational expectations, finding that immigrants showed higher educational expectations than native students and that including relative SES substantially reduced the immigrant paradox. This indicates that incorporating origin-context socioeconomic benchmarks can improve how schools and counselors interpret immigrant students’ educational expectations relative to their achievement.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes Australian PISA extended datasets for 2003 (12,551 students; 321 schools) and 2012 (14,481 students; 775 schools), focusing on mathematics-related constructs for 15-year-olds. The outcomes are math self-concept (weighted total score from PISA items) and educational expectations (a combined scale from binary expectation items). The authors use survey-weighted multilevel random-intercept models with multiple imputation for missing data and plausible values for math achievement, pooling results via Rubin’s rules. Across both cohorts, immigrant students (first- and second-generation) show higher math self-concepts and educational expectations than native students, but the immigrant paradox is reduced when relative SES—operationalized as parents’ origin-country mean years of education—is included. Relative SES negatively predicts both outcomes and helps explain the expectation-achievement gap; school-average achievement shows the expected negative association with self-concept but does not account for the immigrant paradox. Limitations include cross-sectional design and the fact that the paper does not use ML prediction algorithms (it uses multilevel modeling rather than ML).
data.null_fields_interpretation: The manuscript is an empirical multilevel modeling study using survey-weighted random-intercept models, multiple imputation, and plausible values; it does not train or compare machine-learning predictive models. Therefore, ml_techniques.all_techniques is empty and ml_techniques.primary is null by design rather than by omission. As a result, there are no ML performance metrics (e.g., AUC/RMSE) to extract; the reported results are regression coefficients (β) and standard errors from the multilevel models.
